## The idea

[Branch and bound](branch-and-bound.qmd) splits the problem when the LP optimum is
fractional. A cutting-plane method instead **tightens** the relaxation: it finds an
inequality that every integer solution satisfies but the fractional LP optimum violates,
adds it, and solves the LP again. Such an inequality is a **cut**. Repeating moves the
relaxation toward the [integer hull](../modeling-and-formulations/formulation-strength.qmd).

**Example.** In the running example, the first constraint reads
$-5x_1 + 5x_2 \le 14$. Divide by 5: $-x_1 + x_2 \le 2.8$. For integer $x$ the left side
is an integer, so it is at most $2$:
$$
-x_1 + x_2 \le 2 .
$$
No integer point is lost, but the LP optimum $(1.48, 4.28)$, where $-x_1 + x_2 = 2.8$, is
cut off. That is the whole trick: **combine constraints, then round down**.

## Chvátal–Gomory cuts

Let $P = \{x \ge 0 : Ax \le b\}$ and $S = P \cap \mathbb{Z}^n$. Take any multipliers
$u \ge 0$. The combination $u^\top A x \le u^\top b$ is valid for $P$. Since $x \ge 0$,
rounding down the coefficients keeps it valid, and since the left side is then an
integer for integer $x$, the right side can be rounded down too:

::: {.callout-important}
## Chvátal–Gomory inequality
For every $u \ge 0$, the inequality
$$
\lfloor u^\top A \rfloor\, x \;\le\; \lfloor u^\top b \rfloor
$$
is satisfied by every point of $S$.
:::

@gomory1958 introduced cuts of this kind, read off from a row of the optimal simplex
tableau, and showed that a cutting-plane algorithm using them, with suitable rules,
finds an integer optimum after finitely many cuts. @chvatal1973 studied the general
rounding procedure above, which is why the cuts carry both names.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Gomory's fractional cut from the simplex tableau
At an optimal basis, a row of the simplex tableau reads
$x_i + \sum_{j \in N} \bar a_{ij} x_j = \bar b_i$, where $N$ indexes the nonbasic
variables, all equal to $0$ at the LP optimum. If $\bar b_i$ is fractional, write
$f(t) = t - \lfloor t \rfloor$ for the fractional part. Every integer solution satisfies
$$
\sum_{j \in N} f(\bar a_{ij})\, x_j \;\ge\; f(\bar b_i),
$$
while the LP optimum (all $x_j = 0$, $j \in N$) gives $0 < f(\bar b_i)$, so it is cut off.
This is a Chvátal–Gomory cut for a particular choice of $u$ (a row of the basis
inverse), written in terms of the nonbasic variables. Its mixed-integer generalization,
the Gomory mixed-integer cut [@gomory1960], is one of the most effective cuts in solvers
today.
:::

### The cutting-plane loop on the running example

Repeat: solve the LP; find a Chvátal–Gomory cut violated by its optimum; add it. Cuts
may combine earlier cuts as well as the original constraints.

### The closure and the rank

Adding **all** Chvátal–Gomory cuts of $P$ at once gives the **Chvátal closure**
$P'$. Repeating gives $P \supseteq P' \supseteq P'' \supseteq \dots \supseteq
\operatorname{conv}(S)$.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (finite rank)
If $P$ is a rational polytope, then $P^{(t)} = \operatorname{conv}(S)$ for some finite $t$.
:::

This is due to @chvatal1973. The smallest such $t$ is the **Chvátal rank** of $P$; it
measures how far the formulation is from ideal. In the example, $-x_1 + x_2 \le 2$ has
rank 1 (one rounding of the original constraints), while $x_2 \le 3$ and
$x_1 + x_2 \le 5$ were derived from earlier cuts. The rank can grow with the problem
size even for simple problems, which is one reason pure cutting-plane methods stall in
practice: late cuts are nearly parallel to the objective and change the bound very
little.

## Cuts that use problem structure: cover inequalities

General-purpose cuts ignore the meaning of the constraints. Often a single constraint
already has useful structure. Consider a 0–1 knapsack constraint
$\sum_j a_j x_j \le b$ with $a_j > 0$, such as the project-selection budget from
[Modeling with Binary Variables](../modeling-and-formulations/modeling-with-binaries.qmd):
$$
3y_1 + 4y_2 + 2y_3 + 5y_4 + 3y_5 \le 10 .
$$
A set $C$ of items is a **cover** if $\sum_{j \in C} a_j > b$: they cannot all be chosen.
So at most $|C| - 1$ of them can be:
$$
\sum_{j \in C} x_j \le |C| - 1 .
$$
Here $C = \{1, 2, 4\}$ costs $12 > 10$, giving $y_1 + y_2 + y_4 \le 2$. The LP point
$y = (1, 1, 0, 0.6, 0)$ satisfies the budget ($3 + 4 + 3 = 10$) but violates the cover
inequality ($2.6 > 2$).

Cover inequalities, and the conditions under which they define facets of the knapsack
polytope, were studied independently by @balas1975, @wolsey1975 and @hammer1975. They
apply to any constraint row with binary variables, which is why solvers generate them
automatically.

## Separation, and branch and cut

To use a family of cuts we need a **separation** routine: given the LP optimum $x^*$,
find a cut in the family violated by $x^*$, or report that none exists. For
Chvátal–Gomory cuts read from the tableau this is immediate; for covers it is itself a
small knapsack problem, solved heuristically in practice. A deep theorem connects
separation and optimization: for a family of polytopes, one can optimize linear
functions in polynomial time if and only if one can separate in polynomial time
[@grotschel1981].

Cuts and branching work best together. In **branch and cut** [@padberg1991], cuts are
added at the root and at nodes of the
[branch-and-bound](branch-and-bound.qmd) tree, so each node's LP is tighter and more
nodes are pruned. Every modern MIP solver works this way, combining several cut
families: Gomory mixed-integer cuts, covers, flow covers, cliques, and
[lift-and-project cuts](../disjunctive-programming/lift-and-project.qmd) [@balas1993].

## Why it works

A cut never removes an integer point, so the integer optimum is unchanged, while each
cut removes the current LP optimum, so the LP bound can only go down. With the right
family (Chvátal–Gomory cuts on a bounded problem) the process is guaranteed to reach the
integer hull in finitely many rounds. In practice the first few rounds of cuts close
much of the gap cheaply, and branching finishes the job.
